'''''Musa ornata''''', the '''flowering banana''',<ref name=RHSAZ /> is one of more than 50 species of [[banana]] in the genus ''[[Musa (plant)|Musa]]'' of the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Musaceae. Most of these species are large tropical [[evergreen]] [[perennial]]s, mainly from lowland areas with high temperature and humidity. ''Musa ornata'' originated in [[southeast Asia]],<ref>[http://www.tropilab.com/orangebanana.html Tropilab Inc.] - ''Musa ornata''</ref> and is cultivated for its commercial and ornamental value.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20031012074416/http://www.killerplants.com/plant-of-the-week/20030825.asp Killer Plants] - Plant of the Week 25 August 2003: ''Musa ornata''.</ref> The fruit is attractive but tends to be inedible.<ref>[http://charlotte.ifas.ufl.edu/publications/REM-10062009-039--OrnamentalBananas.pdf Ornamental Bananas] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100618161019/http://charlotte.ifas.ufl.edu/publications/REM-10062009-039--OrnamentalBananas.pdf |date=2010-06-18 }} - Not Edible But Beautiful</ref>

==Description==
''Musa ornata'' belongs to the ''[[Musa (plant)|Musa]]'' section ''[[Musa (plant)#Section Musa (incorporating Rhodochlamys)|Rhodochlamys]]''. Rhodochlamys is one of the four sections into
which the genus Musa is divided (the others being Australimusa, Callimusa and Eumusa, which is sometimes called Musa). As a member of Rhodochlamys, ''M. ornata'' has a basic chromosome number of 2n = 22 compared with 2n = 20 of the Australimusa and Callimusa.  Plants of this section are known for their brightly colored bracts.<ref>[http://musalit.inibap.org/pdf/IN030399_en.pdf.asp Diversity in the genus Musa]{{dead link|date=May 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} - Focus on Rhodochlamys</ref>

The true ''M. ornata'' is found in [[India]] and is a small species. From its home in India it reached [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]] early in the 19th century where it became naturalized. ''M. ornata'' is not an especially variable plant in itself but it hybridizes freely with other species. The result is that there are a number of hybrids derived from it in the tropical regions of America.<ref>[http://webebananas.com/bvar-O-Q.html.asp ENCANTO FARMS]{{dead link|date=May 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} - Ornata</ref>

Plants grow to a height of {{convert|5 to 10|ft|m|abbr=on}}. The plants have green [[foliage]] with pink tones throughout. The [[leaves]] can grow to be {{convert|6|ft|m|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|14|in}} wide and can be used for tropical cut [[flower arrangements]]. It produces pink flowers and small, dark pink or [[crimson]] fruit. The fruit type is a banana that is seeded and inedible.<ref>[http://rareseedsource.com/proddetail.php?prod=ornata.asp Rare Seed Source]{{dead link|date=May 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} - Musa Ornata Dwarf Banana Purple Flower</ref>

''Musa ornata'' has a yellow-orange inflorescence whose male and female flowers both tend to be 3-5 per bract in a single row, varying up to about 7 per cluster. The anthers of the male flowers are purple while the female style is green.

==Distribution==
''Musa ornata'' is native to south-east Asia and commonly found in Bangladesh, Burma, and India.  This species is widely distributed throughout tropical regions but it is often misnamed.  The plant is relatively tolerant and was found in Mauritius (off the coast of Madagascar) before 1805 and must have begun to travel several years before it was botanically described in 1824 on Indian banana plantations.  Numerous parts of Mexico have also naturalized the plant, although the seedlings are often offered commercially under a different name (''Musa violacea'').<ref>[http://www.users.globalnet.co.uk/~drc/mornata.htm.asp Musa ornata]{{dead link|date=May 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
==Cultivation==
''Musa ornata'' is one of several banana species grown as ornamental plants for their handsome foliage, for instance in mixed tropical plantings.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|pages=1136}}</ref> In [[temperate]] zones it must be protected from winter frosts, or grown under glass with heat - minimum temperature {{convert|7|C|F|abbr=on}}. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Musa ornata''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/11237/Musa-ornata/Details | access-date = 3 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 65
| publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 4 April 2018}}</ref>  It flowers readily and produces few but viable seeds.

==Other uses==
The male [[bud]] may be cooked or used in salads, while the leaves are often incorporated in making dressings.  The [[root]] of the plant is also sometimes used for ayurvedic preparations ([[alternative medicine]]) in northeast India.  The ash of the [[pseudostem]], the [[corm]], the fruiting stalk and fruit [[Peel (fruit)|peel]] are also used as an anti-scorbutic (to prevent [[scurvy]]), as well as for digestive help, or as a tonic.<ref>[https://docs.google.com/viewer?a=v&q=cache:zDmatgBe-78J:www.erajournal.org/ojs/index.php/era/article/viewFile/360/239+musa+ornata+used+for+decoration&hl=en&gl=us&pid=bl&srcid=ADGEESga2AKDIric13bXckrJlU1byvyVpfafapUDAB3PY4Y-AOL_Rku6eU_gYhZKkv1gVsB9wU8xGd4tKgBfRURRJdv6xSWs9DflKSQBC3Ce62jOSWSjiiNGGb7W7cZ78P0GgNpm7ShI&sig=AHIEtbTJ9KhW7NUj_LXzCD2V_LNfaOmQXg.asp Bananas and People in the Homeland of Genus Musa:Not just pretty fruit]- Jean Kennedy, published July 30, 2009.</ref>
